html:
On 2 February 1659 Jan van Riebeeck, commander of the Dutch station at the Cape of Good Hope, wrote in his diary that wine had been pressed from Cape grapes for the first time. It was the start of South African wine.

The station existed to feed ships of the Dutch East India Company, and wine was thought to help prevent scurvy on long voyages. Vines had been planted a few years after the Dutch settled the Cape. The work in the vineyards was done largely by enslaved people.

The industry grew around Stellenbosch, founded in 1679, and Constantia, the estate of governor Simon van der Stel. French Protestant refugees, the Huguenots, arrived from 1688 and settled at Franschhoek. In the 1700s the sweet wine of Constantia was prized in Europe's courts. South Africa is now one of the world's larger wine producers.
